question_text: A 22-year-old primigravida is admitted to the obstetrics ward with leg swelling at 35 weeks gestation. She denies any other symptoms. Her pregnancy has been uneventful and she was compliant with the recommended prenatal care. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 168/95 mm Hg; heart rate, 86/min; respiratory rate, 16/min; and temperature, 36.7℃ (98℉). The fetal heart rate was 141/min. The physical examination was significant for 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremity. A dipstick test shows 1+ proteinuria. On reassessment 15 minutes later without administration of an antihypertensive, her blood pressure was 141/88 mm Hg, and the fetal heart rate was 147/min. A decision was made to observe the patient and continue the work-up without initiating antihypertensive therapy. Which of the following clinical features would make the suspected diagnosis into a more severe form?

                    ### Question
                    A 22-year-old primigravida is admitted to the obstetrics ward with leg swelling at 35 weeks gestation. She denies any other symptoms. Her pregnancy has been uneventful and she was compliant with the recommended prenatal care. Her vital signs were as follows: blood pressure, 168/95 mm Hg; heart rate, 86/min; respiratory rate, 16/min; and temperature, 36.7℃ (98℉). The fetal heart rate was 141/min. The physical examination was significant for 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremity. A dipstick test shows 1+ proteinuria. On reassessment 15 minutes later without administration of an antihypertensive, her blood pressure was 141/88 mm Hg, and the fetal heart rate was 147/min. A decision was made to observe the patient and continue the work-up without initiating antihypertensive therapy. Which of the following clinical features would make the suspected diagnosis into a more severe form?

                    ### Options

opb. Blood pressure of 165/90 mm Hg reassessed 4 hours later
opc. Hematocrit of 0.55
opd. Platelet count 133,000/μL
ope. Serum creatinine 0.98 mg/dL

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In evaluating the severity of preeclampsia, several clinical features are considered. A 24-hour urinary protein of 5 g/L indicates severe proteinuria, which is a criterion for severe preeclampsia. Persistent hypertension, such as a blood pressure of 165/90 mm Hg reassessed 4 hours later, also suggests severe preeclampsia. A hematocrit of 0.55 suggests hemoconcentration, which can be associated with severe preeclampsia, but is less definitive than other criteria. A platelet count of 133,000/μL indicates thrombocytopenia, a recognized feature of severe preeclampsia. The retrieved evidence supports the association between thrombocytopenia and preeclampsia. A serum creatinine of 0.98 mg/dL is within normal limits and does not indicate severe preeclampsia. Therefore, the most indicative features of a more severe form of preeclampsia in this context are severe proteinuria, persistent hypertension, and thrombocytopenia.
